entity.name: Leonhard Euler
entity.description: The most prolific mathematician in history, with 866 published works. Euler invented modern mathematical notation including f(x), pi, and the imaginary unit i. He went completely blind in his 50s and simply increased his output, dictating roughly one paper per week. Laplace said it best: 'Read Euler, he is the master of us all.'

story.name: Leonhard Euler
story.description: A Swiss prodigy enrolls at university at 13, solves the Seven Bridges of Konigsberg, goes blind and doubles his output, and publishes 866 works spanning every branch of mathematics. The most productive mind in the history of the discipline.

moments.name: Leonhard Euler Is Born in Basel to a Pastor's Family
moments.subtitle: A future mathematical titan enters the world in the city of the Bernoullis
moments.description: On 15 April 1707, Leonhard Euler was born in Basel, Switzerland, to Paul Euler, a Reformed Church pastor, and Marguerite Brucker. His father had studied under the great mathematician Jacob Bernoulli and taught young Leonhard mathematics from an early age. At 13, Euler enrolled at the University of Basel, where he studied under Johann Bernoulli, Jacob's younger brother and one of the foremost mathematicians in Europe. Bernoulli recognized Euler's extraordinary talent and persuaded his father to let the boy pursue mathematics instead of the ministry. Basel would give the world the most prolific mathematician in history.

moments.name: Euler Solves the Seven Bridges of Konigsberg and Invents Graph Theory
moments.subtitle: A puzzle about a Sunday walk creates an entirely new branch of mathematics
moments.description: In 1736, Leonhard Euler published his solution to the Seven Bridges of Konigsberg problem, proving mathematically that it was impossible to walk through the Prussian city crossing each of its seven bridges exactly once. Euler's proof abstracted the problem into a network of nodes and edges, inventing what is now called graph theory and producing the first practical application of topology. The paper, written while Euler worked at the Imperial Russian Academy of Sciences in St. Petersburg, transformed a recreational puzzle into a foundational concept of modern mathematics, computer science, and network analysis.

moments.name: Euler Goes Completely Blind and Increases His Mathematical Output
moments.subtitle: Losing his eyesight only makes the most prolific mathematician faster
moments.description: By 1771, Leonhard Euler had lost the sight in both eyes, having suffered vision problems since his 30s. A cataract surgery on his left eye in 1771 initially restored partial sight, but an infection left him almost totally blind. Rather than slowing down, Euler compensated with an extraordinary memory and mental calculation ability, dictating his papers to assistants. His output actually increased during his blind years: nearly half of his 866 published works were produced after his blindness. He managed complex calculations entirely in his head, including lunar orbit computations that filled entire volumes.
moments.address: Imperial Russian Academy of Sciences, St. Petersburg, Russia

moments.name: Euler Writes 200 Letters Explaining Physics to a Teenage Princess
moments.subtitle: The most popular science book of the 18th century, written by a man who supposedly could not communicate
moments.description: In the early 1760s, while living in Berlin, Leonhard Euler wrote over 200 letters on physics, mathematics, astronomy, and philosophy to Friederike Charlotte of Brandenburg-Schwedt, Frederick the Great's teenage niece. Published as Letters to a German Princess, the collection became the most widely read of all Euler's works, translated into multiple languages and published across Europe and America. The book's success is ironic: Frederick the Great had dismissed Euler as unsophisticated and unable to discuss topics beyond mathematics. The Letters proved Euler could explain complex science with remarkable clarity.

moments.name: Euler Dies Mid-Conversation in St. Petersburg After Calculating a Balloon's Orbit
moments.subtitle: The greatest mathematician of the 18th century dies while doing mathematics
moments.description: On 18 September 1783, Leonhard Euler died suddenly in St. Petersburg at the age of 76. According to the account of his assistant Nicolas Fuss, Euler had spent the day calculating the orbit of the recently discovered planet Uranus and discussing the Montgolfier balloon flights. After dinner, while drinking tea and playing with a grandchild, Euler suffered a brain hemorrhage and died within hours. He had produced 866 publications across virtually every branch of mathematics and physics, a record of productivity unmatched in the history of the field. Papers continued to be published posthumously for nearly 50 years.
